title: “God Never Said That”: The Dangerous Lie That Nearly Broke My Faith (And the Truth That Brought Me Back to Jesus)
paragraphs: “God Never Said That”: The Dangerous Lie That Nearly Broke My Faith (And the Truth That Brought Me Back to Jesus)
If everything really happened for a reason… why did it almost destroy you?
There’s a sentence people say when they don’t know what else to say.
You’ve heard it. Maybe you’ve whispered it through tears. Maybe someone said it to you when your world collapsed and you didn’t have the strength to argue back.
“Everything happens for a reason.”
It sounds comforting… until you’re the one bleeding.

Because if everything happens for a reason, then what reason explains betrayal? What reason justifies abuse? What reason comforts a grieving mother? What reason makes sense of the night you begged God to intervene—and heaven felt silent?
And slowly, quietly, without even realizing it… that sentence starts to twist something inside you.
It begins to reshape how you see God.
Because if everything happens for a reason… then God must have wanted it.
And that’s where the fracture begins.
The Bible never actually says that.
Not once.
Not in Hebrew. Not in Greek. Not in Aramaic.
Search it.
What Scripture does say is something far deeper, far more powerful, and honestly… far more uncomfortable.
In Romans 8:28, the Apostle Paul writes in Greek:
“We know that for those who love God, all things work together for good…”
It doesn’t say all things are good.
It doesn’t say all things were caused by God.
It says God works through all things.
That Greek phrase “συνεργεῖ” (synergei) means to cooperate, to work together, to bring into harmony.
God is not the author of evil… He is the Redeemer of it.
There’s a difference.
And if you don’t see that difference, you will start blaming God for things He came to save you from.
James makes it even clearer:
“Let no one say when he is tempted, ‘I am being tempted by God,’ for God cannot be tempted with evil, and He Himself tempts no one.” (James 1:13)
In the original Greek:
“ὁ γὰρ Θεὸς ἀπείραστός ἐστιν κακῶν…”
God is untemptable by evil.
Meaning evil doesn’t originate in Him.
So no… everything does not happen for a divine reason.
Some things happen because we live in a fallen world.
Some things happen because people choose sin.
Some things happen because darkness is real.
And some things happen because we have an enemy who comes to steal, kill, and destroy (John 10:10).
Jesus never said, “The thief comes so that everything makes sense eventually.”
He said the thief comes to destroy.
But then He said something that changes everything:
“I have come that they may have life, and have it abundantly.”
That’s the tension.
Not everything that happens is God’s will.
But nothing is beyond His redemption.
That’s the Gospel.
Look at Joseph.
Betrayed by his brothers. Sold into slavery. Falsely accused. Forgotten in prison.
Years of pain that didn’t make sense.
But when he finally stood face-to-face with the ones who broke him, he said something profound:
In Hebrew, Genesis 50:20:
“אַתֶּם חֲשַׁבְתֶּם עָלַי רָעָה אֱלֹהִים חֲשָׁבָהּ לְטוֹבָה”
“You meant evil against me… but God meant it for good.”
Notice the distinction.
They meant evil.
God didn’t call it good.
He transformed it into good.
That’s what God does.
He doesn’t excuse the wound… He redeems it.
He doesn’t celebrate the pain… He resurrects something through it.
And nowhere is this clearer than the cross.
Because if “everything happens for a reason” were true in the way people say it… then the crucifixion would mean God wanted the betrayal, the torture, the injustice.
But Scripture shows something deeper.
In Acts 2:23, Peter says Jesus was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God,” but then he turns and says:
“you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men.”
Both truths exist.
God had a plan.
But sinful men committed evil.
And somehow… without endorsing their sin… God used it to bring salvation to the world.
That is not “everything happens for a reason.”
That is “God rewrites what should have destroyed you.”
And maybe that’s what you needed to hear.
Because some of you have been carrying questions you were too afraid to say out loud.
Some of you have been quietly wondering why God allowed something that broke you.
Some of you have been trying to force meaning onto pain that never came from Him.
And it’s been exhausting.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
You don’t have to pretend here.
Jesus can handle your honesty.
He already knows.
And He didn’t come to shame you… He came to restore you.
Because the truth is… your story isn’t over.
The worst thing that ever happened to you is not the final sentence.
God is still writing.
Still healing.
Still redeeming.
Still turning ashes into something that breathes again.
And if this opened your eyes even a little, don’t keep it to yourself.
Someone in your life is silently believing a lie about God right now… and it’s slowly pulling them away from Him.
Not to expose them… but to rescue them.
You’re going to need this reminder again on a day when the pain feels louder than the truth.
And if you feel something stirring in your spirit… don’t ignore it.
Stay close to truth.
Because there are more people waking up, more chains breaking, more hearts returning to Jesus… and you’re not meant to walk this alone.
If you’re serious about going deeper, about understanding Scripture without distortion, about growing in real discipleship and not just surface-level faith…
And for those who step in, we’ve made it easier.
If you truly want to glorify God, don’t just read truth—help it reach others.
Because silence doesn’t save people.
The Gospel does.
And you’re part of that.
Because someone out there is one post away from coming back to Jesus… and God might use you to reach them.
Not everything that happened to you came from God… but everything you surrender to Him can still be used by God.
